title: The Church and Political Power Through History: A Five-Session Study
subtitle: A pastoral five-session study on how the church has lived with political power, from a coin held up to trap Jesus to the end of Christendom, keeping the crucified King above every throne.
summary:
This study is for small groups, adult classes, and anyone who feels the ground shifting under the faith in their country and wants to know what is actually dying and what isn't. It works through five of my essays on the long marriage of church and empire: the coin held up to trap Jesus, the three centuries the church grew with no power at all, the teaching of two kingdoms, and the slow end of the arrangement that made Christianity the default religion of the West. It explains the hard words plainly and never sneers at the believer who grieves the change. A busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer rather than argument.

It doesn't flatter the people who want to seize the culture or the people who want to flee it. It asks the Christian reaching for the levers of the state whether he has mistaken a borrowed majority for the work of the Spirit, and it asks the Christian who has washed his hands of public life whether he has called retreat holiness. I'm not outside this either. I've heard the render line preached as a permission slip, I've seen flags stand on platforms no one would move, and part of me misses the store that closed on Sunday.
audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

sessions.title: What Render Unto Caesar Actually Means
sessions.aim: To recover Jesus' words about Caesar's coin as a fence around a coin, not a wall between faith and public life, and to ask what we've quietly handed to Caesar that was never his.
sessions.summary:
They brought Jesus a coin because they wanted him dead. The Pharisees and the Herodians, who agreed on almost nothing, set a trap with one question: should we pay taxes to Caesar or not? Say yes and lose the crowd that hated Rome. Say no and hand the governor a charge of sedition. We've often turned his answer into a permission slip, two tidy drawers, one for politics and one for prayer.

Look at what he actually does. He asks whose likeness is on the coin. It's Caesar's, so give it back. But Genesis says human beings are made in the image of God, and the Greek word Mark uses for Caesar's likeness, eikon, is the word the Greek Old Testament uses there. If the coin belongs to the one whose image it bears, so do we. The comfortable reading isn't foolish; it helped keep church and state from swallowing each other after Europe's religious wars, and Caesar really does have a domain. The question is its size. The line doesn't split reality in half. It puts a fence around a coin and gives everything else to God. Tertullian read it that way: give the coin to Caesar and yourself to God. And they killed Jesus anyway, charging him with forbidding tribute to Caesar.

keyScripture.why: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's" (Mark 12:17). Spoken to escape a trap, the sentence doesn't divide faith from public life. It gives Caesar his coin and gives God everyone who bears his image.

discussion.q: Before tonight, how had you heard "render to Caesar" used? What did it seem to permit?
discussion.behind: Bring the comfortable reading into the open before questioning it. Most will have heard it as "keep your faith out of politics" or "keep your head down." You're not shaming that reading, only showing that the room arrived with the same tidy drawers.

discussion.q: Read Mark 12:13-17. The coin bears Caesar's likeness. Read Genesis 1:27. What bears God's image? What changes when you weigh the two drawers instead of assuming they're the same size?
discussion.behind: This is the center of the session. If what bears God's image belongs to God, Caesar's drawer holds metal and God's holds every person who ever lived, including Caesar. Help the room see that the line doesn't split reality in half.

discussion.q: The two-drawer reading protected real things, helping to keep the church from becoming the state after Europe bled over religion. How do we honor what it got right while seeing what it hid?
discussion.behind: Keep things fair early. The instinct to separate church and state was wisdom paid for in blood, not cowardice. Let the room grant Caesar a real domain before shrinking it, so the conclusion doesn't sound like the church grabbing for Rome's power.

discussion.q: A church with no power might hear Jesus' answer as a challenge to Caesar. A church with power might hear it as a peace treaty. Why would safety change how we hear the same words?
discussion.behind: The words didn't change; the readers did. Help people notice how easily comfortable people tame dangerous texts, and what it would cost to hear this one the way the first listeners did.

discussion.q: What have you quietly handed to Caesar that was never his? Your final allegiance, your sense of who holds history, your hope?
discussion.behind: Move from interpretation to self-examination. Go first if the room is slow. You're not after confessions that shame anyone, only for each person to name one place their deepest trust has drifted toward a power they can see.

objections.objection: This is just a way to drag the church into politics. Jesus told us to render to Caesar so we'd stay in our lane and keep faith private.
objections.response: Notice what the "lane" reading protects before answering it. It guards against the church becoming the state, and that's a real mercy. But the argument here isn't that the church should take Caesar's throne. It's that Jesus' answer keeps Caesar out of the human soul, not faith out of public life. You can give the coin back and still refuse to give the emperor what he most wants, the last word over a person made in the image of God.

objections.objection: Fine, then everything belongs to God, so a faithful Christian should resist paying taxes and treat the government as Pharaoh.
objections.response: That's the opposite error. Jesus didn't lead a tax revolt. The coin goes back, and Peter says, "Fear God. Honor the emperor" (1 Peter 2:17) in a single breath. Jesus' answer puts Caesar in his place without abolishing him. The point isn't to treat every government as an enemy. It's to refuse the one allegiance that belongs to God alone. Pay the tax, and keep nothing of yourself in Caesar's hand.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is one ordinary loyalty in your life that you've never stopped to ask whether it belongs to Caesar or to God?
sessions.practice: This week, whenever you pull out a card or a bill to pay for something, let it prompt a short question: what else have I been handing over without noticing, my final hope, my sense of who's in charge? Don't try to fix it. Just notice where your allegiance went, and write down what it told you.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we've used a hard sentence to make ourselves comfortable, and we've handed you small change while keeping the throne for ourselves. Forgive us for the parts of our hope we've given to Rome. You stamped your image on us, and we belong to you, not to Caesar, not to a party, not to our fear dressed up as prudence. Help us give the coin back to the world this week, and give ourselves wholly to you. In the name of the King the empire couldn't keep buried, amen.
reflection: Where have I read a dangerous text as a safe one because meaning it would cost me nothing?
What have I put in Caesar's drawer that bears God's image?
If my final allegiance were tested tomorrow, do I know where it would land?
sessions.teaching:
Let's start where the trap started, because the setting is half the meaning. They brought Jesus a coin because they wanted him dead. Mark says the authorities "sent to him some of the Pharisees and some of the Herodians, to trap him in his talk" (Mark 12:13). Those two groups agreed on almost nothing. The Pharisees resented Roman rule; the Herodians did well under it. Yet they came together with flattery, "Teacher, we know that you are true and do not care about anyone's opinion," and then the question: "Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?" (Mark 12:14). Say yes and lose the crowd that hated Rome. Say no and hand the governor a charge of sedition. There was no safe answer. That's what a trap is for.

Keep that in mind, because we've often taken one of the most dangerous sentences in the Gospels and turned it into a permission slip. "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's" (Mark 12:17), and we hear two tidy drawers, one for politics and one for prayer. Many of us have preached it or heard it that way, as if Jesus came to teach us to keep our heads down. I don't think the text will let us.

Watch what he actually does. "Why put me to the test? Bring me a denarius and let me look at it" (Mark 12:15). It says something that he has to ask for one and they have one to hand. The denarius of the day carried the face of the emperor Tiberius and an inscription calling him son of the divine Augustus. "Whose likeness and inscription is this?" he asks. "Caesar's," they say (Mark 12:16). The word for likeness is eikon, and it's the same word the Greek Old Testament uses when "God created man in his own image" (Genesis 1:27). The coin bears Caesar's image, so give it back to him. But the question left hanging in the air is what bears the image of God. The answer is the person holding the coin.

Before pressing that, give the comfortable reading its due, because it isn't foolish. The two-drawer reading protected real things. It helped keep the church from becoming the state and the state from becoming the church, and after Europe bled through its wars of religion, the instinct to keep the spheres apart looked like mercy. It was. Caesar has a domain, and taxes are real. Jesus didn't lead a tax revolt, and Peter tells Christians in one breath to "Fear God. Honor the emperor" (1 Peter 2:17).

So answer the strong version. Yes, Caesar has a domain; the question is its size. The two-drawer reading assumes the drawers are about equal, with God holding the soul and Caesar holding the body, the budget, and the army. But weigh the sentence again. If what bears God's image belongs to God, then Caesar's drawer holds metal stamped with his face, and God's drawer holds every person who has ever lived, including Caesar. The line doesn't divide reality in half. It puts a fence around a coin and gives everything else to God. Tertullian saw this in the early third century. In his treatise On Idolatry he reads the passage as giving Caesar's image on the coin to Caesar and God's image in the person to God, so that you give Caesar your money and give God yourself, since if everything were Caesar's, nothing would be left for God.

And they killed him anyway. The charge brought to Pilate was the very one the trap was built to produce: "We found this man misleading our nation and forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king" (Luke 23:2). Rome understood something we tend to miss. A man who says the emperor himself bears the image of a higher King hasn't stayed out of politics. He has refused the emperor the last word.

A church without power tends to hear this as a challenge to Caesar. A church with power tends to hear it as a truce, and for much of the last sixteen centuries we've been the church with power. The words didn't change. What changed was who was reading them and what it would cost to mean them. So the trap meant for Jesus springs on us instead. Not whether we'll pay our taxes; we will, and we should. The question is what we've quietly handed to Caesar that was never his: our final allegiance, our sense of who holds history, the part of us that votes its fear and calls it prudence. Give the coin back. Keep nothing of yourself in his hand.

scriptureStudy.note: "They sent to him some of the Pharisees and some of the Herodians, to trap him in his talk." Two factions who distrusted each other unite only to get rid of Jesus. The trap is the frame of the whole saying.
"Teacher, we know that you are true and do not care about anyone's opinion." The flattery is the bait before a question with no safe answer.
"Why put me to the test? Bring me a denarius and let me look at it." Jesus won't pretend the question is sincere, and it's his questioners who have the coin.
"Whose likeness and inscription is this?" The word is eikon, the word for "image." The whole answer is waiting in it.
"So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him." The coin bears Caesar's image and goes back to Caesar. The person bears God's image and belongs to God.
"Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's. And they marveled at him." The sentence fences a coin and gives every image-bearer to God.
"Forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king." Jesus' answer didn't get him off the hook. Rome heard what comfortable readers miss.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a group that wants more, think about what the denarius was. The coin carried Tiberius's image and an inscription naming him son of the divine Augustus, a small claim of imperial divinity in every pocket. Many devout Jews found such images offensive, which helps explain why the Pharisees resented the tax while the Herodians profited from the arrangement.

Then take up the contested history of the two-drawer reading. In The Myth of Religious Violence, William Cavanaugh argues that the tidy split between religious and secular wasn't a neutral discovery but a story the rising modern state told about itself, presenting itself as the calm referee that ended religious violence. Hold that argument at its weight; don't swallow it whole or wave it away. Ask whether our instinct to keep faith private is Christian wisdom or a settlement we accepted from a rival power. Set beside it N. T. Wright's reading that confessing "Jesus is Lord" was never only a private devotion in a world where Caesar claimed lordship. And work out the difference between putting Caesar in his place and abolishing him, since the same passage that shrinks the emperor also tells us to pay the tax.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a thoughtful member of your group, a quiet professional who avoids conflict, has clearly found relief in the comfortable reading. When you press it, he pushes back gently. He's always loved this verse, he says, because it lets him keep his faith out of the office, off social media, and away from the dinner table where his family argues about politics. He keeps his head down, votes privately, and takes Jesus' words as a blessing on exactly that.

He isn't grasping for power. He's doing the opposite: handing the whole of public life to Caesar and calling it obedience. Honor what's wise in his instinct, because a faith that becomes a culture war is its own disease and he's right to fear it. Then show him gently that the line he loves was never a wall between faith and public life. It was a fence around a coin, and everything that bears God's image, including the conversations he avoids, sits on God's side of it. Retreat isn't the same as rendering to God.

devotional.title: Why They Brought the Coin
devotional.body:
"And they sent to him some of the Pharisees and some of the Herodians, to trap him in his talk" (Mark 12:13). They didn't bring Jesus a coin to learn something. They brought it to be rid of him. The question had no safe answer: say pay the tax and lose the crowd, say don't and hand Rome a charge of treason.

We've softened a sentence spoken inside a trap into a tidy rule for keeping faith private. A sentence spoken to escape a death trap reads differently from a slogan on a mug. Today, notice whether you've taken some of Jesus' hardest sayings and filed them in a safe drawer that asks nothing of you. Let this one be dangerous again before you let it comfort you.
devotional.prayer: Lord, I've made your hard words easy and called it understanding. Let me hear this one where you spoke it, in the shadow of the cross.

devotional.title: Whose Image
devotional.body:
Jesus asks whose likeness is on the coin, and they say Caesar's. The Greek word is eikon, the same word the Greek Old Testament uses when "God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him" (Genesis 1:27). The coin bears Caesar's image, so it goes back to Caesar. But you bear God's image.

That means the question isn't only what you owe the government. It's whose you are. Caesar can have his coin. He can't have the person, because the person was stamped by someone else. Today, let that be both a claim and a comfort. You belong to God, and no power that has its face on your money has its face on you.
devotional.prayer: Father, you made me in your image, and I'm yours. Let me give the world what belongs to it, and give myself to you.

devotional.title: The Size of Caesar's Drawer
devotional.body:
The comfortable reading isn't foolish. It helped keep the church from becoming the state, and after Europe's religious wars that looked like mercy. Peter says, "Honor everyone. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the emperor" (1 Peter 2:17). Caesar has a real domain.

The question is its size. If every person bears God's image, Caesar's drawer holds metal, and God's holds everyone who has ever lived. Today, honor the authorities over you in the ordinary ways Scripture asks, and then notice how small their claim is next to God's. Fear God. Honor the emperor. The order of those two isn't an accident.
devotional.prayer: Lord, help me honor those in authority without giving them what is yours. Keep the emperor in his place in my heart.

devotional.title: A Sword or a Truce
devotional.body:
At his trial they accused Jesus of "forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king" (Luke 23:2). Rome heard the challenge in his answer. A man who says the emperor bears the image of a higher King has refused the emperor the last word.

A church without power tends to hear Jesus' words as a challenge to Caesar. A church with power tends to hear them as a truce. The words don't change; the hearers do. Today, ask whether your own safety has softened how you hear Jesus, and what it would cost you to hear him the way his first listeners did.
devotional.prayer: Lord Jesus, they killed you for words I've made comfortable. Give me ears to hear what Rome heard.

devotional.title: What You Handed Over
devotional.body:
In the wilderness the devil showed Jesus "all the kingdoms of the world and their glory" and offered them for one act of worship, and Jesus answered, "You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve" (Matthew 4:8-10). The trap with the coin was the same offer on a smaller scale. Give Caesar the coin, yes, but the trap wanted the allegiance too, and that Jesus wouldn't give.

End the week by asking what you've quietly handed to Caesar that was never his: your final hope, your sense of who holds history, your fear dressed as prudence. Give the coin back. Keep nothing of yourself in his hand.
devotional.prayer: Lord, show me what I've handed over without noticing. Take back what is yours, all of me. Amen.

sessions.title: Christendom Is Ending. Christianity Is Not.
sessions.aim: To tell Christendom, a social arrangement, apart from Christianity, the people who confess a crucified Lord, and to grieve the right one.
sessions.summary:
Many pastors say the country is losing its faith, and they mean it as a funeral. Attendance falls, the number of people claiming no religion grows, and the assumption that a decent person is probably some kind of Christian has nearly disappeared. It's natural to grieve, until you notice two different things being grieved under one word. Christianity is the people who confess that Jesus is Lord. Christendom is the arrangement in which that confession is a civilization's default, built into its laws, calendar, and manners. One is dying. The other has outlived empires before.

Jesus compared the kingdom to a mustard seed, the smallest of seeds that becomes a tree. The parable promises growth from smallness, not ownership of the field. Christendom's defenders aren't foolish. It built hospitals and universities and a moral language the secular world still borrows, and Oliver O'Donovan argues the gospel really did reshape political authority. But it also built a Christianity you could inherit without ever meeting Christ, which Kierkegaard spent his last years attacking. The arrangement has a date: Constantine's victory at the Milvian Bridge in 312, and by 380 Nicene Christianity was the official religion of the empire. The end of Christendom isn't the defeat of the church. It may be its return to the conditions under which it first grew.

keyScripture.why: "The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his field. It is the smallest of all seeds" (Matthew 13:31-32). Jesus promises life that grows from smallness, not a tree that owns the field. Christendom forgot the difference.

discussion.q: We often use one word, Christianity, for two things, the faith and the cultural arrangement around it. Where do you see the two confused, in your own life or around you?
discussion.behind: Get the distinction into the room in plain terms. The faith is people who confess a crucified Lord. Christendom is the setting where that confession is the default. The rest of the session depends on telling them apart.

discussion.q: Read Matthew 13:31-33. What does the mustard seed promise, and what doesn't it promise? Why might the church have assumed for centuries that it meant something bigger?
discussion.behind: Help people feel the distance between what Jesus described and what the church became. He pointed to the smallest thing in the garden, and in time the church built the largest thing in the empire.

discussion.q: Christendom built real goods, hospitals, universities, a moral language the secular world still uses. How do we honor those goods while still asking what we're really grieving?
discussion.behind: Keep things fair. Christendom's defenders aren't cartoon theocrats; they've seen what replaces a Christian frame and found it wanting. Make sure no one who grieves the change feels mocked before the harder point comes.

discussion.q: Kierkegaard attacked a Christianity everyone had simply by being born in the right country. Where have you seen faith made cheap because it was the default?
discussion.behind: This is the heart of the session. When faith is the default, the word stops meaning anyone in particular. Help people see, without contempt, that some of what's falling away now is the nominal and inherited.

discussion.q: Many of us would like the old scaffolding back, the full pews and the easier job, even knowing that habit and respectability filled some of those pews. Where do you feel that pull?
discussion.behind: Close by turning inward, leader first. The confession many of us need to make is that we miss the advantage and call it missing the faith. Don't rush anyone to a tidy answer.

objections.objection: This is a convenient way to celebrate the collapse of Christian culture. The decline of faith is a tragedy, and calling it freedom is just spiritualizing defeat.
objections.response: The loss is real, and it shouldn't be flattened. Grieve the hospitals if they close and the mercy if it sours, and fight for those, because they're good. The claim here is narrower. Cultural Christianity isn't the same thing as the church, and part of what's dying is the nominal and the convenient. You can mourn the real losses without putting the church in the coffin, because the seed is still in the ground.

objections.objection: If Christendom built the hospitals and the universities and the moral language, then pulling out the Christian root will rot the fruit. We should defend the arrangement, not bury it.
objections.response: That's a strong argument, and O'Donovan is right that the gospel bent the West into new shapes of mercy and law. The question is whether the church protected those goods by being the church or by leaning on the state. A consensus held by habit is always a generation away from collapse. The deeper answer isn't to defend a throne. It's to form a people who would keep living the mercy when the culture no longer requires it. That's the church the early centuries produced.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: When you picture the faith you want to hand the next generation, are you picturing a culture that supports it or a community that lives it?
sessions.practice: This week, notice one thing you've always assumed was Christian about your surroundings, a phrase, a holiday, a habit, a store closed on Sunday. Ask whether it points anyone to the crucified Lord or only to a culture that used to call itself by his name. Bring what you find to the next session.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord of the small seed, we've mistaken the tree we built for the kingdom you planted, and we've grieved the loss of our advantage as though it were the loss of you. Teach us to tell the church from the culture that wore its clothes. Where cheap faith is falling away, give us the costly kind that has met the offense of the cross. You grew your church under a hostile empire once. Grow it in us again. Amen.
reflection: When I grieve the changes in my country, am I grieving the loss of Christ or the loss of an advantage?
Where has my faith been cheap because it was the default?
If every cultural support for my faith were gone tomorrow, what of it would still be standing?
sessions.teaching:
Let's begin with the funeral, because that's how the change feels to many faithful people. Pastors say the country is losing its faith, and they mean it as a death. The surveys back them up: attendance falls, and the number of people who claim no religion grows. The old assumption that a decent person is probably some kind of Christian has thinned to almost nothing. The grief is natural.

But notice that we're grieving two different things with one word. There's Christianity, the people who confess that Jesus is Lord and order their lives around a crucified man who walked out of a tomb. And there's Christendom, the social arrangement in which that confession is the default setting of a civilization, built into its laws and calendar and manners, so that belonging to the culture and belonging to the church feel like the same thing. One is dying. The other has outlived empires before.

Jesus told a parable that's older than the problem. "The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his field. It is the smallest of all seeds, but when it has grown it is larger than all the garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and make nests in its branches" (Matthew 13:31-32). Notice what it doesn't promise. It doesn't say the tree will own the field, pass the laws, or seat the king. It promises growth from smallness, life from something you could lose in the dirt. Jesus described his movement as the smallest thing in the garden, and for much of its history the church assumed he meant the largest thing in the empire.

Christendom's defenders deserve a full hearing, because they aren't power-hungry theocrats. They've looked at what replaces a Christian frame and found it wanting. They point out, rightly, that the hospital, the university, and the very idea that the weak have worth grew in soil Christendom tilled. Oliver O'Donovan, in The Desire of the Nations, argues that political authority itself was reshaped by the gospel, that the West was bent by Christianity into new shapes of mercy and law. When people like that grieve, they're grieving something real. Scaffolding is coming down, and scaffolding holds things up.

So answer the strong version. Yes, Christendom built hospitals and universities and a moral language the secular world still borrows. But the same arrangement built something the gospel never asked for, a Christianity you could inherit without ever meeting Christ. When faith is the default, it's cheap, and the word stops meaning anyone in particular. Søren Kierkegaard spent his last years attacking exactly this in nineteenth-century Denmark, a Christendom where everyone counted as a Christian simply by being born Danish, and almost no one had faced what he called the offense of a crucified Lord. Some of what's dying now is the very thing he was trying to kill from the inside.

The arrangement has a date. In 312, before the battle at the Milvian Bridge, Constantine reportedly saw a sign, won the battle, and soon ended the persecution of the church. In 380 the Edict of Thessalonica made Nicene Christianity the official religion of the empire. In about three generations the faith went from a persecuted minority burying its martyrs to an establishment that could, in time, persecute others. The end of persecution was a genuine mercy. It was also the moment the mustard seed began to be mistaken for a cedar.

Here's what grief often can't see. The end of Christendom isn't the defeat of the church. It's the church's return to the conditions under which it first learned to grow. The loss is real. I have five sons who are inheriting a thinner world than I did, and I understand wanting the old scaffolding back, the full pews and the easier job. But we have to admit what filled some of those pews. Habit filled them, and respectability filled them. Those aren't the gospel. So grieve the right thing: grieve the hospitals if they close and the mercy if it sours, and fight for those. But don't grieve the end of cultural Christianity as though the church were in the coffin. "Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit" (John 12:24). The seed is still in the ground.

scriptureStudy.note: "The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his field." The first word about the kingdom is smallness and hiddenness, a seed lost from sight, not a banner over a capital.
"It is the smallest of all seeds, but when it has grown it is larger than all the garden plants." The growth is real, even large, but it comes from below, through burial and patience.
"The seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how." The kingdom grows by a hidden life the farmer can't engineer. Christendom tried to manufacture the growth by law and calendar.
"The kingdom of heaven is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, till it was all leavened." Leaven works unseen and from within, not by visible power from above.
"We preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles, but to those who are called ... Christ the power of God." A crucified Lord makes a poor mascot for a comfortable culture.
"But you are a chosen race ... I urge you as sojourners and exiles." The church's early way of seeing itself is exile, not establishment, and that's the posture it's learning again.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a group that wants more, weigh the history of the Constantinian shift carefully. Popular accounts treat 312 as either a glorious triumph or a simple fall, and both are too clean. In Defending Constantine, Peter Leithart argues against the tidy story of decline, holding that the emperor's conversion was more genuine and its effects more mixed than critics allow. Let that voice stand against Stanley Hauerwas and William Willimon's Resident Aliens, which reads the end of the Constantinian arrangement not as a death to mourn but as the church being freed to be faithful again.

Ask what each account assumes about how God works in history, through the spread of Christian institutions or through a faithful minority that doesn't need them. Then bring in Lesslie Newbigin, who returned to Britain in 1974 after decades as a missionary in India and found his own country had become a mission field. His question reframes the session: how does the gospel speak to a culture that thinks it already knows what the gospel is and has moved on? Notice the difference between a missionary posture, which asks how to bear witness again, and a restoring posture, which asks how to recapture institutions. This study supports public engagement and refuses the recapture.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a respected older couple in your group, faithful for decades, grieve the changes in the country with real tears. The wife says she doesn't recognize the world her grandchildren are growing up in. The stores are open on Sunday, the schools teach things she can't accept, and she has started giving to a ministry that promises to put Christian leaders back in charge of the culture and win the country back for God. She isn't retreating. She's reaching hard for the levers.

Her grief is real and her love for her grandchildren is real, and you should say so first. Then put the session's gentle question into her hands: is she grieving the loss of Christ or the loss of an advantage? The arrangement she wants back filled pews with habit and respectability as well as faith. Don't shame her longing. Show her that the church grew fastest when every cultural lever pulled the other way, and that a faith held up by the culture is always a generation from collapse.
