devotional.title: Two Words for One Thing
devotional.body:
"For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God" (Colossians 3:3). We grieve the country losing its faith, and we often use one word for two things. Christianity is the people whose life is hidden with Christ. Christendom is the arrangement in which that faith was a culture's default.

One is dying. The other can't be killed by a culture's changing mind, because its life is hidden somewhere no culture can reach. Today, ask which of the two you've been leaning on. Your life isn't hidden in a country's habits. It's hidden with Christ.
devotional.prayer: Lord, let my life be hidden with you, not propped up by the world around me.

devotional.title: The Smallest Seed
devotional.body:
Jesus compared his kingdom to "a grain of mustard seed ... the smallest of all seeds" (Matthew 13:31-32). It grows into a tree, but it starts as something you could lose in your hand, and nothing in the parable promises the tree will own the field.

The church has often wanted the field. Today, look for the small things God may be growing in you and around you, a prayer, a friendship, an act of mercy, and don't despise them for being small. That's how the kingdom has always started.
devotional.prayer: Lord of the small seed, teach me not to despise small beginnings, and to trust what you grow in hidden places.

devotional.title: When Faith Is Cheap
devotional.body:
To the church in Sardis the risen Christ says, "You have the reputation of being alive, but you are dead" (Revelation 3:1). A reputation for faith is easy to have when the whole culture calls itself Christian. Kierkegaard spent his last years attacking a Christendom where everyone counted as Christian simply by being born in the right place.

When faith is the default, it's cheap. Today, ask whether any part of your faith is a reputation more than a life, something you have because of where you were raised rather than because you've met Christ. If so, he hasn't given up on you. To Sardis he says, "Wake up."
devotional.prayer: Lord Jesus, wherever my faith is only a reputation, wake me up and make it alive.

devotional.title: What Filled the Pews
devotional.body:
God says through Hosea, "Your love is like a morning cloud, like the dew that goes early away" (Hosea 6:4). Many of us would like the old scaffolding back, the full pews and the store closed on Sunday. But we should admit what filled some of those pews: habit, respectability, the fear of being the odd family on the street.

That kind of faithfulness burns off like morning dew once the culture stops requiring it. Today, ask what's holding your faith in place. If the culture's approval disappeared, would your love for God disappear with it, or would it hold?
devotional.prayer: Lord, I don't want a faith that evaporates when the weather changes. Root my love in you.

devotional.title: The Seed Is Still in the Ground
devotional.body:
"Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit" (John 12:24). Grieve the right things: grieve the hospitals if they close and the mercy if it sours, and work to protect them. But don't grieve the end of cultural Christianity as though the church were in the coffin.

Jesus taught that life comes through burial. What looks like death may be a seed going into the ground. End the week by handing God your grief for what's being lost, and asking him for eyes to see what he may be planting.
devotional.prayer: Lord, you bring life out of the ground. Take my grief, and show me what you're planting. Amen.

sessions.title: The Early Church Under Rome: Faith Without Power
sessions.aim: To look at the three centuries the church grew with no army, no protective law, and no social standing, and to ask whether we still know how to be that church.
sessions.summary:
Around the year 112, Pliny the Younger, a Roman governor, wrote to the emperor Trajan asking how to handle the Christians he kept executing. He couldn't name a crime. What he punished was their stubbornness, their refusal to make the small civic gesture that would have saved them. That's the church we forget. For nearly three hundred years, from the cross to Constantine, it had no army, no friendly law, and no protection, and it grew.

Paul described that life from the inside: "afflicted in every way, but not crushed" (2 Corinthians 4:8). Rome deserves a fair hearing. It tolerated many religions, and it read the Christian refusal as disloyalty dressed up as piety. But what Rome saw as corrosion was a different kind of community growing inside the old one, one that treated slaves and senators as the same kind of creature, took in infants left to die, and stayed with the sick during plagues. The sociologist Rodney Stark argued that Christians' care during the plagues helped the church grow. When you can't compel, you can only attract.

keyScripture.why: "We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed" (2 Corinthians 4:8-9). Paul names the gap between what the empire could do to the body and what it couldn't do to the hope.

discussion.q: Pliny executed Christians not for a crime he could name but for refusing a small civic gesture. Why was a pinch of incense worth dying over to them?
discussion.behind: Start with what the empire actually asked. Rome rarely demanded a change of belief, only a gesture that showed the state held your final loyalty. The Christians understood that the gesture was the point. They'd already given that loyalty to Christ.

discussion.q: Read 2 Corinthians 4:7-12. What's the difference between not being crushed and winning? Why do we keep confusing the two?
discussion.behind: The early church wasn't winning and wasn't crushed, and those are different claims. We often act as though hope requires victory. Help the room feel the freedom of a faith that doesn't need to be winning to be alive.

discussion.q: Rome had real reasons to see the church as a threat, a group that wouldn't fit back into the civic religion. How do we take that seriously instead of treating the persecutors as cartoon villains?
discussion.behind: Honor the empire's logic. If you believed the gods kept the harvest and the borders safe, a movement that insulted them looked dangerous. Rome wasn't simply evil. The church offered a rival way of life, and that's what scandalized it.

discussion.q: Stark argued that the church grew in part because Christians stayed and cared for the dying during plagues while others fled. What does it tell us that the faith spread so widely when it had so little power?
discussion.behind: When you can't compel, you can only attract, and what attracted people was bodies that stayed, tables where unlikely people ate together, infants taken in. Help the group see that powerlessness made the love visible.

discussion.q: Many of us fear a future where faith costs our children something. The early church had already lost the safety and standing we're trying to protect. What are you most afraid of losing?
discussion.behind: Close by turning inward. Let people name what they fear losing, and ask whether the church Pliny couldn't explain had it at all. Go first.

objections.objection: Romanticizing persecution is easy from a comfortable pew. Suffering isn't a strategy, and wishing the church back into the catacombs is spiritual tourism.
objections.response: That's a fair warning, and it's why the cost should be traced with dates rather than sentiment: Nero after the fire of 64, the martyrs of Lyon in 177, the empire-wide demands under Decius in 250, the Great Persecution under Diocletian from 303. Suffering isn't something to celebrate or chase. The point is narrower. The church did some of its clearest work when it had no power, so we shouldn't assume it can't grow without an advantage it did without for three centuries.

objections.objection: If powerlessness is so holy, then Christians should stay out of public life entirely and let the world run itself while we tend our own pure community.
objections.response: The early church itself rules that out. The first Christians didn't withdraw into private piety. They built a visible community inside the old one, took in the discarded, stayed through plagues, and refused the empire's idolatry openly at the cost of their lives. Faith without power isn't faith without engagement. A church that attracts because it can't compel is more public, not less.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: When have you been drawn to a community not by an argument it made but by the way it treated people everyone else ignored?
sessions.practice: This week, do one thing the early church was known for that needs no power or platform. Stay with someone others avoid, care for someone the culture has written off, or quietly meet a need no law requires you to meet. Notice what it asks of you.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, the church you grew had no army, no law, and no place to stand, and it outlasted the empire that killed it. We've leaned so hard on safety and standing that we hardly know how to be the church without them. Take away our fear of losing what Rome never gave the first Christians. Make our love visible the way theirs was, in people who stay when others leave. You had a tomb that wouldn't stay shut. It was enough then. Let it be enough for us. Amen.
reflection: If my faith could no longer compel anyone and could only attract, would there be anything attractive left?
Where am I trusting a safety and standing the early church never had?
What small gesture would I make to stay comfortable, and what does that say about my final loyalty?
sessions.teaching:
Let's begin with a puzzled governor, because Rome's confusion tells us what the church was. Around the year 112, Pliny the Younger, governing a province in what is now northern Turkey, wrote to the emperor Trajan asking how to handle the Christians brought before him. He'd been asking them three times whether they were Christians. Those who denied it he had invoke the gods, offer incense and wine before the emperor's image, and curse Christ. Those who persisted he sent to execution. He couldn't name a crime. What he punished was their stubbornness itself, their refusal to make the one small civic gesture that would have saved them. Read that letter and you meet the early church the way Rome met it, not as a comfortable majority but as a problem for an official with the power to kill.

That's the church we tend to forget. We picture cathedrals and councils and bishops writing to kings as equals. But for nearly three hundred years, from the cross to Constantine, the church had no army, no friendly law, no social standing, and no guarantee that confessing Christ wouldn't cost a life. It was faith without power, and it grew.

Paul described that life from the inside. "We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed" (2 Corinthians 4:8-9). The word that carries it is "but." The faith lived in that small word, in the gap between what the empire could do to the body and what it couldn't do to the hope. They weren't winning, but they weren't crushed. Those are different claims, and we've often acted as if the second depended on the first.

Rome deserves a fair hearing, because it wasn't a cartoon villain. By ancient standards it was tolerant of religion, absorbing gods the way it absorbed provinces. What it couldn't absorb was a group that refused to be absorbed, that wouldn't add the emperor to its gods or offer the small sacrifice that marked you as a safe member of society. From Rome's side this looked like disloyalty dressed up as piety. If you believed the gods kept the harvest coming and the borders secure, a movement that taught people to scorn them was a public danger. Robert Louis Wilken's The Christians as the Romans Saw Them shows how educated Romans made exactly that case.

But what Rome read as corrosion was what made the church grow. Christians didn't spread by offering a better civic religion. They offered what the empire couldn't: a community that treated a slave and a senator as the same kind of creature, that took in infants left exposed to die, that cared for the sick in plague years when many fled. In The Rise of Christianity, Rodney Stark argued that this care, along with ordinary friendships and families, helped the church grow, because Christians who stayed and nursed the sick saw more of their people survive and won the gratitude of neighbors. Tertullian reports pagans saying of Christians, in effect, look how they love one another. Jesus had said, "By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another" (John 13:35). When you can't compel, you can only attract, and when no law enforces your ethic, it has to be lived in the open or it doesn't exist.

There's a detail worth slowing down for. Rome rarely demanded that Christians stop believing. It demanded a gesture, a pinch of incense, and under Decius in 250, a certificate proving you'd sacrificed. The empire didn't much care what you held privately. It cared whether you'd perform the public act that showed your final loyalty belonged to the state. Christians died over the gesture because they understood it was the whole point. It asked for the one thing they'd already given to Christ.

Here's where it turns toward us. We assume the church needs power to do its work. The first three centuries suggest otherwise. The church did some of its clearest work, and grew remarkably, when it had no power at all. Powerlessness made the love visible. Once the church gained the empire, the love became harder to see, because you could no longer tell who had come for Christ and who had come for Constantine.

scriptureStudy.note: "We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair." Paul isn't describing victory. He's describing a hope the pressure can't reach.
"Persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed." The empire could do the first half of each phrase to the body. It couldn't touch the second half.
"But we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us." The power is visible precisely because the vessel is plainly breakable.

"Always carrying in the body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our bodies." The cross isn't an accident that happens to the church. It's how the life becomes visible.
"By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another." When you can't compel, love is the whole argument.

"And they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death." Tertullian would later say that the blood of Christians is seed. The martyrs' witness was their victory.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a group that wants more, test the romance out of persecution before drawing lessons from it. Trace the cost with dates. Nero blamed the Christians for the fire of 64. Eusebius records the martyrs of Lyon in 177 in painful detail. Under Decius in 250, every citizen had to obtain a certificate of sacrifice. The Great Persecution under Diocletian began in 303.

Then ask whether the church grew because of the suffering or despite it. Stark's sociological answer is worth weighing rather than simply accepting. He argues that growth came less from martyrdom than from ordinary networks of family and friends, higher birth rates, the refusal to expose infants, and the greater survival of Christians and those they nursed during the great plagues of the second and third centuries. The martyrs' witness was real, but the unspectacular daily life of a different community may have done more. Then take up the harder question. If powerlessness made love visible, is power always a corruption, or did the church gain something real when it could build hospitals and schools on a large scale? Resist both the triumph story that reads Constantine as pure gain and the nostalgia that treats the first three centuries as the only faithful church. The aim is to learn what faith without power knew, not to invent a persecution we don't have.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a sincere young man in your group has been reading about the early church and reached a conclusion that worries you. The lesson is clear, he says: the church was pure when it stayed out of the world and was corrupted the moment it engaged, so the faithful thing now is to pull back, build a small holy community, and stop wasting energy on the public square and the wider world.

His instinct against grasping for power is right, and you should honor it. But the early church refutes his conclusion as firmly as it refutes the power grab. The first Christians didn't withdraw into private piety. They built a visible community inside the old one, took in the discarded, stayed through plagues, and refused the empire's idols openly. Faith without power wasn't faith without engagement. Show him that the Christians he admires were among the most visible people in the empire, not the most hidden.

memoryVerse.text: We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed.

devotional.title: The Puzzled Governor
devotional.body:
"Yet if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in that name" (1 Peter 4:16). Around 112, a governor named Pliny wrote his emperor asking what to do with the Christians he kept executing. He couldn't name a crime. They simply wouldn't make the small civic gesture that would have saved them.

Most of us will never face that choice. But we face smaller ones: the moment to stay quiet about Christ, the small compromise that keeps us comfortable. Today, notice one of those moments, and ask whether the name of Christ is something you're glad to carry or something you quietly set down when it costs you.
devotional.prayer: Lord, let me never be ashamed of your name. Give me the courage of the people Pliny couldn't understand.

devotional.title: Afflicted But Not Crushed
devotional.body:
"We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair" (2 Corinthians 4:8). The whole faith lives in that small word "but." It marks the gap between what the empire could do to the body and what it couldn't do to the hope.

Paul doesn't say he's winning; he says he isn't crushed. Those are different things. Today, whatever is pressing on you, name it honestly, and then add Paul's "but." You may be afflicted. You aren't abandoned.
devotional.prayer: Lord, in what presses on me today, give me Paul's "but." Let my hope rest where no pressure can reach it.

devotional.title: When You Cannot Compel
devotional.body:
"By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another" (John 13:35). The early church had no law to enforce its way of life, so it had to be lived in the open or it didn't exist. For three centuries, that love was the argument the empire could see.

When you can't compel, you can only attract. Today, ask what someone watching your life would see. Not your opinions, but the way you treat people others overlook. That's still the argument the world can read.
devotional.prayer: Lord Jesus, make my love visible enough that someone watching would think of you.

devotional.title: The Pinch of Incense
devotional.body:
Three young men told King Nebuchadnezzar, "If this be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us ... But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden image that you have set up" (Daniel 3:17-18). Rome, like Babylon, rarely asked believers to stop believing. It asked for a gesture, a pinch of incense, a few words to the emperor.

The early Christians understood that the gesture was the point. It asked for the loyalty they'd already given to Christ. Today, look for the small gestures you make to fit in, the things you say or don't say to stay comfortable, and ask whether any of them gives away what belongs to God.
devotional.prayer: Lord, give me the courage of "but if not." Let me give no gesture of worship to anything but you.

devotional.title: A Tomb That Would Not Stay Shut
devotional.body:
"And with great power the apostles were giving their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all" (Acts 4:33). The power Luke means wasn't an army, a law, or a seat at the table. It was an empty tomb and a grace that rested on ordinary people.

The early church had no power in the world's sense, and it outlasted Rome. End the week by asking what you're really depending on. If the resurrection was enough for them, it's enough for you.
devotional.prayer: Risen Lord, your empty tomb was enough for the first Christians. Let it be enough for me. Amen.

sessions.title: Two Kingdoms: How Christians Relate Faith and State
sessions.aim: To recover the teaching of two kingdoms as a way of holding a tension, honoring the office while judging the officeholder, rather than a wall that silences the church or a license that blesses the state.
sessions.summary:
Christians often ask whether they should care about politics, and behind the question are two opposite fears: that the church has become a wing of a party, and that saying no would abandon the poor, the unborn, and the prisoner. Both fears are right, and the old language of two kingdoms was built to hold them together. God rules the world in two ways, through the church by the word and through the civil order by law and the sword, and the two shouldn't collapse into one.

The teaching has been abused in both directions. Paul's command, "Let every person be subject to the governing authorities" (Romans 13:1), was written to Christians in Nero's Rome, and the same passage calls the ruler "God's servant for your good" (Romans 13:4). A servant has a job, and a job can be failed. The strongest case for separation is wisdom paid for in blood: the crusades, the inquisitions, the wars of religion. Augustine answered from inside the tradition with two cities mixed together in history. And in the 1930s, when much of the German church had sealed the two kingdoms into separate rooms, the Confessing Church declared at Barmen that Jesus Christ is the one Word of God we must obey. Two kingdoms, one Lord.

keyScripture.why: "For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. ... for he is God's servant for your good" (Romans 13:3-4). The passage that commands submission also defines the ruler's job, and that lets the church say when a ruler has failed it.

discussion.q: Behind the question "Should Christians care about politics?" are two fears, that the church has become a party's chaplain and that it will abandon the vulnerable. Which fear do you feel more strongly, and why?
discussion.behind: Get both fears into the room. Both are legitimate, and the teaching of two kingdoms exists to hold them together. Notice which fear the room leans toward, because that shows which mistake it's more likely to make.

discussion.q: Read Romans 13:1-7. Paul commands submission, and he also calls the ruler God's servant for good. How does a defined job become a job that can be failed?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge. The text used to bless tyrants is the same text that puts the state on a leash. If the ruler is God's servant with a task, the church can say when the servant has betrayed the master. Submission and judgment live in the same passage.

discussion.q: The strongest case for keeping church and state apart is the history of crusades, inquisitions, and religious wars. What is that separation rightly guarding against?
discussion.behind: Honor the separation before complicating it. A church that holds the sword stops persuading and starts coercing, and a state that claims God's sanction becomes a god with an army.

discussion.q: In the 1930s much of the German church treated the two kingdoms as sealed rooms, and that silence helped a terrible regime go unchallenged. How does the teaching rightly understood do the opposite?
discussion.behind: This is the turn at the center of the session. Rightly understood, the two kingdoms don't free the state from judgment. They place it under a higher court and give the church somewhere to stand. Barmen is the model.

discussion.q: Where have you seen, or felt in yourself, a faith so tied to a political program that it could no longer rebuke it?
discussion.behind: Close by turning inward, leader first, and keep it pointed in every direction. The chaplain who can't rebuke the power he loves comes in conservative and progressive versions.

objections.objection: Two kingdoms is just a clever way to tell the church to keep quiet and stay in its lane while the state does as it pleases. It silences the prophets.
objections.response: That's the abuse the German church fell into, two kingdoms as two sealed rooms, and the teaching rightly understood reverses it. If the state is God's servant with a defined job, the church is exactly the body that can say when the servant has failed. The distinction isn't a wall protecting the state from the church's voice. It's the place where the church stands to tell Caesar he isn't God. Only a church that knows it belongs to a different kingdom can speak prophetically to this one.

objections.objection: If the church really believes the gospel, it should take up the state's power and use it to make the country righteous. Why leave the sword to unbelievers?
objections.response: The cross rules that out. When Peter drew his sword in the garden, Jesus said, "Put your sword back into its place. For all who take the sword will perish by the sword" (Matthew 26:52). A gospel enforced by the sword is no longer the gospel. The two-kingdoms discipline isn't passivity. It means serving the city, paying the tax, honoring the office, and working for justice while keeping one foot in the kingdom of the crucified King, so that when the city asks to be worshiped, the church has somewhere to stand and the words to refuse.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Is there a political power you love so much that you'd find it hard to rebuke it, even when it was clearly wrong?
sessions.practice: This week, look for one place where you've tied the gospel so closely to a political program that you can't tell them apart. Practice honoring the office while judging the officeholder by naming one thing your own side has done that the cross condemns. Write down whether you can still see the seam between your faith and your party.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you rule the church by your word and the world by law and the sword, and you are the one Lord over both. We've collapsed the two into one, sometimes silencing your church to keep the peace, sometimes seizing the state to win. Forgive us for the tables where we traded our voice for a seat. Help us serve the city, pay the tax, and honor the office, while keeping one foot planted with the crucified King, so that when the city asks us to bow, we have somewhere to stand. Two kingdoms, one Lord. Amen.
reflection: Am I more tempted toward a church that grabs the state's sword or a church that falls silent before it?
Where have I tied the gospel so closely to a program that I can't rebuke the power I love?
Do I honor the office while still judging the officeholder, or has my side decided in advance what I'm willing to call wrong?
sessions.teaching:
Let's start with a common question and the two fears behind it, because both fears are right and this teaching exists to hold them. Christians often ask whether they should care about politics. Some are afraid the church has become a wing of a party, praying in a campaign's colors. Others are afraid that saying no means abandoning the poor, the unborn, and the prisoner to whatever the powerful decide. That's what the old language of two kingdoms was built for. Put simply, God rules the world in two ways at once: through the church by the word and the sacraments, and through the civil order by law and the sword. These aren't the same rule, and they mustn't collapse into each other. Like most old ideas, it's been abused in both directions, used to tell the church to stay out of public life and used to let the state do as it pleased.

Take the passage everyone quotes and few read whole. "Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God" (Romans 13:1). That sentence has been used to bless tyrants for centuries. But Paul wrote it to Christians in Rome, a city where, within a decade, Nero would put believers to death after the great fire. And he didn't write a blank check. He gave the ruler a job: "For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. ... for he is God's servant for your good" (Romans 13:3-4). The word for servant is diakonos, someone under orders. The text that commands submission is the same text that defines the job, and a job defined is a job that can be failed.

The strongest case for keeping church and state apart isn't cowardice. It's wisdom paid for in blood. The people who most want faith and state kept distinct have often read the most history. They know what happened when the church held the sword: crusades, inquisitions, and the wars of religion that turned much of Europe into a graveyard. They know a church with state power stops persuading and starts coercing, and a gospel enforced by the sword is no longer the gospel. They aren't telling the church to be silent. They're telling it not to pick up the sword.

Augustine answered from inside the tradition. After the Goths sacked Rome in 410, he wrote The City of God, describing two cities, one formed by love of God and one by love of self, mixed together in history until the end and told apart by their loves rather than their borders. He didn't tell Christians to abandon the earthly city. He told them to seek its peace and serve it, without mistaking it for home. Jeremiah had told the exiles the same: "seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile" (Jeremiah 29:7). You can love your country and still know it isn't your King.

The cross works against both abuses at once. A church that grabs the state's sword forgets that its Lord told Peter, "Put your sword back into its place. For all who take the sword will perish by the sword" (Matthew 26:52). And a state that claims the church's authority forgets that the only throne the church recognizes belongs to a man Rome executed. Stand at the cross and you can't bless the sword, and you can't silence the church either. "We must obey God rather than men" (Acts 5:29).

The teaching also has a graveyard. In the 1930s, a decayed form of two-kingdoms thinking had settled into a tidy division of labor in much of the German church: the church tends the soul, the state tends everything else, and the church has no business judging the state in its own sphere. Many historians believe that habit of mind helped a church stay quiet while a regime did what it did. In 1934 the Confessing Church declared at Barmen, in a text drafted largely by Karl Barth, that Jesus Christ is the one Word of God we must hear and obey in life and in death, and it rejected the false teaching that there are areas of life in which we belong to lords other than him. The two kingdoms had become two sealed rooms, and the sealing let evil rule one room unchallenged.

So here's the turn. People reach for the two kingdoms to get the church out of politics, but the teaching rightly understood does the opposite. It doesn't free the state from judgment. It places the state under a higher court. If the ruler is God's servant with a defined job, the church is the very body that can say when the servant has betrayed the master. Scripture shows both faces of the same Rome: God's servant in Romans 13, and a beast demanding worship in Revelation 13. Only a church that knows it belongs to a different kingdom can tell Caesar he isn't God. Two kingdoms, one Lord. Forget the second part and you've lost the point.

scriptureStudy.note: "Let every person be subject to the governing authorities." Written to Christians in Nero's Rome. A real command to submit, and the verses that follow put the ruler under orders.
"For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad." The ruler is given a purpose. A ruler who terrifies the good and protects the wicked has stepped outside the job this text gives him.
"For he is God's servant for your good." The word is diakonos, a servant under orders. A servant has a master and a task, and a servant can be unfaithful.
"Put your sword back into its place. For all who take the sword will perish by the sword." The church's Lord refused the sword at his own arrest.
"We must obey God rather than men." Submission is real but not absolute. When the servant commands what the master forbids, the higher loyalty governs.
The same Rome that Romans 13 calls God's servant appears here as a beast demanding worship. The authority that serves God can become the authority that plays God.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a group that wants more, follow the history of the idea so it doesn't flatten into a slogan. Two-kingdoms language runs through Augustine's two cities, takes sharp form in Luther's distinction between God's rule through the gospel and his rule through civil authority, set out in his treatise on temporal authority in 1523, and develops differently again in the Reformed and Anabaptist traditions. Each guards against a different danger, and each can be bent in a different way. In the wrong hands, the Lutheran version can decay into a quietism that tells the gospel to govern the soul while the state governs the world without spiritual accountability. The theocratic temptation runs the other way, collapsing the two so the church wields the sword directly.

Read the Barmen Declaration of 1934 closely, especially its first two articles. Set beside it Bonhoeffer's Ethics, written in the years of the German church's failure, where he criticizes thinking in terms of two separate spheres. Then ask whether Barmen abolishes the two kingdoms or rescues them. This study's answer is that it rescues them: the distinction isn't a wall that silences the church but the place from which the church can tell the state it isn't God.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose an energetic newer believer in your group is impatient with all this talk of tension and restraint. The country is sliding into evil while Christians sit on their hands, he says. God has given the church the truth and the votes to fix it, so the faithful thing is to take power, capture the courts and the legislatures and the schools, and use the state to make the nation righteous. Why leave the sword to unbelievers?

His zeal for righteousness is real, and his frustration with a passive church isn't wrong. Honor both before you complicate them. Then show him that the cross rules out his plan. The church that grabs the sword forgets its Lord refused it. The two-kingdoms discipline isn't the passivity he despises. It's serving the city, honoring the office, and working hard for justice while keeping one foot in the kingdom of the crucified King. The sword he wants would cost him the gospel he means to defend.

memoryVerse.text: Then Jesus said to him, "Put your sword back into its place. For all who take the sword will perish by the sword."

devotional.title: Two Fears at Once
devotional.body:
"He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the LORD require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?" (Micah 6:8). When Christians ask whether to care about politics, two fears pull at them: that the church has become a party's chaplain, and that stepping back would abandon the vulnerable.

Micah holds both. Justice and kindness are required, and so is humility. Today, ask which of the two fears you feel more, and what Micah's three requirements would ask of you this week, in your own town and with your own neighbors.
devotional.prayer: Lord, teach me to do justice, love kindness, and walk humbly with you, without making any party my god.

devotional.title: A Leash, Not a Blank Check
devotional.body:
"For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. ... for he is God's servant for your good" (Romans 13:3-4). Paul wrote those words to Christians in Rome, not long before Nero turned on them. He commanded submission, and in the same breath he gave the ruler a job.

A servant has a master and a task. That's why Christians can honor those in authority and still say when they've failed. Today, pray for those who govern you, by name if you can, and pray that they'll do the job God gave them.
devotional.prayer: Lord, I pray for those who govern me. Make them servants for good, and give me the courage to say so when they aren't.

devotional.title: Two Cities, One Age
devotional.body:
"Seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf, for in its welfare you will find your welfare" (Jeremiah 29:7). After Rome fell in 410, Augustine wrote of two cities mixed together in history, one formed by love of God and one by love of self, told apart by their loves rather than their borders.

He didn't tell Christians to flee the earthly city. He told them to seek its peace without mistaking it for home. Today, do one concrete thing for the good of the place where you live, and remind yourself as you do it that it isn't your final home.
devotional.prayer: Lord, help me seek the good of my city and love it well, while keeping my heart set on your kingdom.

devotional.title: The Sword in the Garden
devotional.body:
When the soldiers came for Jesus, Peter drew his sword. Jesus said, "Put your sword back into its place. For all who take the sword will perish by the sword" (Matthew 26:52). He refused the sword at the moment it seemed most justified.

The church keeps forgetting this. When we're sure our cause is right, we reach for whatever power will win. Today, notice where you're tempted to win by force, whether with words, influence, or pressure, and ask what it would look like to follow the Lord who put the sword away.
devotional.prayer: Lord Jesus, you put away the sword. Help me put away mine.

devotional.title: One Word We Must Obey
devotional.body:
"We must obey God rather than men" (Acts 5:29). In 1934 the Confessing Church declared at Barmen that Jesus Christ is the one Word of God we must hear and obey, and that there is no area of life in which we belong to another lord. They said it because much of the German church had sealed the gospel into a private room and left the state to do as it pleased.

Two kingdoms, one Lord. End the week by asking whether there's any area of your life you've quietly handed to another lord, your work, your politics, your money, and give it back to Christ.
devotional.prayer: Lord Jesus, you are Lord of every part of my life. Show me what I've given to another lord, and take it back. Amen.

sessions.title: The Church After Cultural Power
sessions.aim: To face the fact that the church no longer sets the terms of the culture, and to ask the harder question of whether it knows how to be the church without them.
sessions.summary:
The store used to close on Sunday because the whole town agreed the day belonged to God, and now it doesn't, and some Christians feel that as the end of the world. Many of us grew up at the tail end of an arrangement where the culture did half the church's work for free. That's gone. The question isn't how to get it back but whether the church knows how to be the church without it. Much of what we mourn as the loss of faith may be the loss of advantage.

Jesus said, "You are the salt of the earth, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored?" (Matthew 5:13). Salt is useful because it's different from the dish, and the danger isn't that the world overpowers it but that it dissolves. The grief deserves respect. Real goods eroded when the culture stopped honoring the faith. But the church often protected those goods by borrowing the state's power rather than by forming people, and a consensus held that way doesn't last. The end of cultural Christianity is a test of what's left when the advantage is gone.

keyScripture.why: "You are the salt of the earth, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled under people's feet" (Matthew 5:13). Salt loses its use not when the world overpowers it but when it dissolves until no one can taste the difference.

discussion.q: Much of what we mourn as the loss of faith may be the loss of advantage. Where do you feel the difference between grieving Christ and grieving the home-field edge?
discussion.behind: Say the hardest claim of the session gently. Some of the decline is people who never believed no longer pretending. Help the room separate the loss of faith from the loss of cultural support without dismissing the pain in either.

discussion.q: Read Matthew 5:13-16. Jesus warns about salt that loses its taste. How might a church slowly dissolve into the culture around it?
discussion.behind: The danger is sameness, not hostility: the same fears, the same hopes, the same securities as everyone else. Salt does its work by being different.

discussion.q: People mourning the church's lost cultural place are often mourning real things, protection for the unborn, care for the poor, support for marriage. How do we take that grief seriously and still ask the harder question?
discussion.behind: Keep things fair. Make sure no one feels their grief is being mocked before the harder point comes, that some of those goods were held by borrowed power rather than changed hearts.

discussion.q: Why is a majority built on cultural habit weaker than it looks? What's the difference between winning votes and making disciples?
discussion.behind: A consensus held by habit can be undone by one election, because it rests on power rather than persuaded hearts. Formation is slower than legislation, and much sturdier.

discussion.q: Some churches respond to the loss by fighting to recapture the levers. Others quietly build communities so different that neighbors ask what makes them that way. Which is more natural to you, and which do you want to hand to the next generation?
discussion.behind: Close with a real choice, leader first. This study isn't neutral about it, and neither are you, but ask for an honest answer, not a performance. Let people name which response they've actually been living.

objections.objection: So the answer is for Christians to retreat into pure little communities and give up on the public square, abandoning the vulnerable to whoever stays in the fight.
objections.response: No. The community this study points to isn't a bunker. It's a people so different that the watching world is drawn to them, who take in the discarded and live differently in public. The early church had no cultural power and wasn't withdrawn; it was one of the most visible communities in the empire. Losing the levers isn't the same as leaving the world. It's finding out whether the church can be salt without the wind at its back.

objections.objection: If Christendom protected the unborn and the poor and marriage, then losing it is a disaster, and the faithful thing is to fight to get cultural power back.
objections.response: Those goods were real, and they're worth fighting for. The question is how the church held them, by being the church or by borrowing the state's power to compel. A protection that rests on a majority rather than on changed hearts is always one election from collapse, and the church often mistook that borrowed strength for its own. The deeper work is forming a people who'll keep living the mercy when the law no longer requires it. That's the only kind of strength the early church had.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If the culture stopped doing any of the church's work for you tomorrow, what part of your faith would simply stop, and what would keep going?
sessions.practice: This week, do one thing that makes you different rather than blended in, an act of mercy, truthfulness, or generosity that the culture around you doesn't explain or reward. Don't announce it. Notice whether your faith can act without the wind of approval at its back, and write down what you learn.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, the culture is done carrying us, and we're afraid, because we've leaned on it so long we aren't sure what's underneath. Forgive us for trusting the levers more than the cross, for counting votes when you called us to make disciples. Make us salt that keeps its taste, a people so marked by you that a watching neighbor has to ask what makes us this way. You grew your church once with every cultural lever pulling the other way. Do it again in us. Amen.
reflection: How much of my religion has depended on advantage, and how much of my witness could survive without it?
Have I been fighting to recapture the levers, or helping build a community different enough to be noticed?
When the culture stops doing the church's work, what will be left of my faith?
sessions.teaching:
Let's start at the closed store, because that's where the grief lives. The store used to close on Sunday because the whole town agreed the day belonged to God. Now it doesn't, and some Christians feel that as the end of the world. That's understandable. Many of us grew up at the tail end of an arrangement where the culture did half the church's work for free, where the calendar, the schools, and the social pressure all leaned the same way the sermon did. That arrangement is gone. The church no longer sets the terms. The real question isn't how to get the terms back. It's whether the church knows how to be the church without them.

This is hard to say to grieving people. Much of what we mourn as the loss of faith may be the loss of advantage. For a long time we had the home-field edge: the assumption that decent and Christian meant nearly the same thing, and a social cost for leaving rather than for staying. Take that away and attendance falls, not only because people stopped believing but because some who never really believed stopped pretending. Part of the decline is the nominal and the convenient falling away. It hurts, and it's also a kind of truthfulness arriving late.

Jesus said, "You are the salt of the earth, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled under people's feet" (Matthew 5:13). We hear the first part as a compliment and skip the warning. Salt is useful because it's different from the dish. The danger Jesus names isn't that the world will overpower the salt. It's that the salt will become indistinguishable from what's around it. In many ways Christendom was a long temptation to dissolve, to blend into the culture so completely that no one could taste the difference.

The grief deserves a fair hearing, because it isn't foolish. People who mourn the church's lost place are often mourning real losses. When the culture honored the faith, there were more protections for the unborn, more institutions caring for the poor, more support around marriage. Those were goods, and a flippant Christianity that celebrates their loss as freedom has stopped loving its neighbors. That grief is love looking at a wound.

So answer the strong version. Yes, those were goods, and their erosion is a real wound. But the question is whether the church protected them by being the church or by borrowing the state's power to compel, and the difference matters. When a good is protected by a cultural consensus rather than by people whose hearts have changed, the protection is always one election from collapse, because it rests on power rather than persuasion. The church sometimes mistook a borrowed majority for its own strength. It learned to win by counting votes instead of making disciples, and a victory won that way can't be kept.

The cross shows what we were trusting. A crucified Lord is the permanent answer to the idea that the kingdom advances by holding the levers. Jesus held none. He had no majority and no favorable law, and the crowd he did encounter called for his death. "For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God" (1 Corinthians 1:18). A church that grieves its lost power is, without meaning to, admitting that it had begun to trust the levers more than the cross.

I include myself in this. We say we want the culture back so we can serve our neighbors better, and some of that is true. But some of it is that losing power has shown how much of our religion was power, how little of our witness could survive without the wind at our backs. The end of cultural Christianity is a test of whether anything is left when the advantage is gone. Churches tend to respond in two ways. Some grow frightened and pour their energy into recapturing the levers. Others, more quietly, stop waiting for the culture to do their work and start doing it themselves: forming people, taking in the discarded, building communities so different that a neighbor has to ask what makes them that way. The first looks like an effort to restore Christendom. The second looks like the people Pliny couldn't explain. "Our citizenship is in heaven" (Philippians 3:20). The culture is done carrying us. Now we find out what we believe.

scriptureStudy.note: "You are the salt of the earth." Salt exists to be different from the dish, to season and preserve by not blending in.
"But if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored?" The danger isn't that the world overpowers the salt but that the salt dissolves.
"It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled under people's feet." The trampling comes after the salt has forgotten what it was for.
"You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden." The witness is meant to be visible and distinct, not hidden and not blended.
"For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God." The kingdom's power is the cross, not the lever.
"But our citizenship is in heaven." The church learns again to live as exiles, serving the city without mistaking it for home.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a group that wants more, press the diagnosis further. In To Change the World, James Davison Hunter argues that the church's main strategies for influencing culture, political conquest on the right and activism on the left alike, share a flawed theory of how cultures change: too much confidence in politics and ideas, too little attention to the slow work of institutions and networks. His alternative, which he calls faithful presence, is worth weighing. Ask whether this study's picture of a distinct community and Hunter's faithful presence are the same proposal or differ in important ways.

Set beside Hunter William Cavanaugh's argument, in Theopolitical Imagination, that the modern church too easily accepts the role the state assigns it, a private supplier of values, forgetting that it is itself a public body with its own way of life. Then ask whether the loss of cultural power is best read as catastrophe, opportunity, or judgment. The most truthful answer may be all three. Finally, take the hardest counterpoint seriously. If the old consensus really protected the vulnerable, losing it is a real harm, and the call to slow formation could accept that harm too lightly. Don't romanticize powerlessness. Ask whether faithful presence can protect the vulnerable or whether it quietly gives up the field.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a capable woman in your group, once active in every ministry, has gone quiet and a little bitter. When you reach the question about the two responses, she says she's done. She fought the culture wars for twenty years, made the calls, marched, voted, and lost. Now she's decided the world will do what it wants, and the only sane thing is to tend her own garden, raise her kids, and stop caring what happens out there.

She isn't reaching for the levers. She's dropped them and called the despair peace. Her exhaustion is real; she has carried more than most, and you should honor that. But her retreat is the mirror image of the recapture she gave up, and the early church answers both. The alternative to the culture war was never the walled garden. It was salt, lived in the open, visible enough that a neighbor has to ask. Show her gently that withdrawing isn't the rest she thinks it is.

memoryVerse.text: You are the salt of the earth, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled under people's feet.

devotional.title: The Loss of Advantage
devotional.body:
"Salt is good, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is of no use either for the soil or for the manure pile. It is thrown away" (Luke 14:34-35). Much of what we mourn as the loss of faith may be the loss of advantage, the social edge Christians once had. When that edge disappears, some who never really believed stop pretending.

That hurts, and it's also a kind of truthfulness. Today, ask what part of your own faith has depended on the advantage. If it disappeared, would the salt still have its taste?
devotional.prayer: Lord, keep my faith salty when the advantage is gone. Let it depend on you, not on the culture's approval.

devotional.title: Salt That Dissolves
devotional.body:
"Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind" (Romans 12:2). Salt loses its use not when the world overpowers it but when it dissolves into the dish. That was the long temptation of Christendom, to blend so thoroughly into the culture that no one could taste the difference.

Today, look for one place where you've simply taken on the fears, hopes, and habits of everyone around you. Ask God to renew your mind there, so that your life tastes of something the world doesn't produce on its own.
devotional.prayer: Lord, don't let me dissolve into the world around me. Renew my mind, and make my life taste of you.

devotional.title: Love Looking at a Wound
devotional.body:
"Open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are destitute. Open your mouth, judge righteously, defend the rights of the poor and needy" (Proverbs 31:8-9). The grief over the church's lost place isn't foolish. When the culture honored the faith, the unborn, the poor, and families had more support. Those were real goods.

That grief is love looking at a wound. Don't let anyone shame you out of it. Today, turn that grief into one concrete act for someone who can't speak for themselves.
devotional.prayer: Lord, turn my grief into care for those who can't speak for themselves.

devotional.title: A Borrowed Majority
devotional.body:
"Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts" (Zechariah 4:6). When a good is protected by a cultural majority rather than by changed hearts, it's always one election from collapse. The church sometimes learned to win by counting votes instead of making disciples.

God's work has never finally depended on might or power. Today, ask where you've trusted a majority more than the Spirit, and pray for one person you could help grow as a follower of Jesus.
devotional.prayer: Lord, not by might or power, but by your Spirit. Teach me to trust your Spirit more than any majority.

devotional.title: Now We Find Out
devotional.body:
"For it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God" (1 Peter 4:17). The culture is done carrying the church. Now we find out what we believe. Losing power has shown how much of our religion was power, and how little of our witness could stand without the wind at our backs.

That's a hard word, but judgment that begins with God's household is also mercy, because it comes while there's still time to change. End the week by asking God to show you what in your faith has depended on the culture, and to build something in you that will stand without it.
devotional.prayer: Lord, begin with me. Show me what in my faith leaned on the culture, and build in me a faith that stands on you alone. Amen.

leaderPrimer:
History feels safe, and that's the trap in this study. A group can talk about Rome, Constantine, and Pliny's letter all evening with real pleasure and go home untouched, because empire always seems to be somebody else's sin: a Roman problem, a medieval problem, at worst the other party's problem. Your main job across these five sessions is to close that distance. When the room looks at the church that gave Caesar its blessing in exchange for standing, it's looking at us. Lead from inside the loss rather than above it.

Expect two kinds of grief at your table. Some people are mourning cultural power: the country they remember, the assumption that being decent meant being churched. Their grief is real, even where memory is kinder than the record. Others carry the opposite wound, hurt by a church so tied to power that it could no longer tell the gospel from the flag. Don't referee a contest between those griefs. Put the denarius on the table in front of both, because Jesus was handed a trap and answered with a coin and a question about whose image it bore (Mark 12:13-17), and everything in this study follows from that.

The hardest sessions are two and five, where the end of Christendom stops being an idea and becomes someone's funeral. Let people say what they're afraid of. Then keep pointing to the early church, which had no legal standing, no buildings, and no friendly emperor, and turned the world over anyway, not because weakness is a strategy but because the church has never needed Caesar's permission to be the church. You aren't leading a seminar on the decline of an institution. You're helping people see that what they thought was dying was scaffolding, and that what the scaffolding held is alive. Lead calmly, unhurried and unafraid of the news.

faq.q: Is this study just telling Christians to keep their faith private and stay out of politics?
faq.a: No. Jesus' words about Caesar's coin were never a wall between faith and public life. They put a fence around a coin, and everything that bears God's image, which is nearly everything, belongs to God. The study grants the whole case for engagement: the prophets confronted kings, and a church that washes its hands of power has often abandoned the people power crushes. The error it names isn't engagement but the belief that engagement means seizing the throne. And it questions the Christian who hands the public square to Caesar and calls that holiness just as firmly.

faq.q: Isn't this just a way to bless political passivity and keep Christians pure?
faq.a: It would be if it spared the quietist, and it doesn't. The session on the early church answers the retreat directly. The first Christians built a visible community inside the old one, took in the discarded, stayed through plagues, and refused the empire's idols openly at the cost of their lives. Faith without power wasn't faith without engagement. A church that attracts because it can't compel is more public, not less.

faq.q: What does "render to Caesar" mean, if not "keep faith out of politics"?
faq.a: Jesus was handed a coin in a trap meant to get him killed, and he asked whose likeness was on it. Caesar's, so give it back to Caesar. But the Greek word for likeness, eikon, is the word the Greek Old Testament uses when Genesis says human beings are made in God's image. The coin bears Caesar's image and goes back to him. The person bears God's image and belongs to God. The line doesn't divide reality in half. It fences a coin and gives every image-bearer to God. So the question isn't whether you'll pay your taxes; you will. It's what you've quietly handed to Caesar that was never his.

faq.q: Should Christians really not panic about the end of Christendom?
faq.a: The study refuses both panic and celebration. Christendom is the arrangement in which Christianity was a civilization's default, built into its laws and calendar. Christianity is the people who confess a crucified Lord. One is ending; the other has outlived empires before. Some of what we mourn is the loss of advantage, the nominal no longer pretending. But the study doesn't flatten the grief. Grieve the hospitals if they close and the mercy if it sours, and fight for those. Just don't put the church in the coffin. The church first grew under a hostile empire with no cultural lever in its favor.

faq.q: Were the centuries of persecution really better than the church having power?
faq.a: The study is careful not to romanticize suffering. It traces the cost with dates: Nero after the fire of 64, the martyrs of Lyon in 177, the demands under Decius in 250 and Diocletian from 303. The point isn't to chase martyrdom. It's narrower. The church did some of its clearest work when it had no power, because powerlessness made its love visible. That isn't an argument that suffering is holy. It's a warning against assuming the church needs a safety and standing it did without for three hundred years.

faq.q: Does the two-kingdoms teaching tell the church to keep quiet while the state does as it pleases?
faq.a: That's the abuse the study names directly, the German church of the 1930s, where two kingdoms became two sealed rooms. Rightly understood, the teaching does the reverse. If the state is God's servant with a defined job, the church can say when the servant has failed. The Confessing Church said it at Barmen in 1934: Jesus Christ is the one Word of God we must obey. Two kingdoms, one Lord.

faq.q: If the gospel is true, shouldn't the church use political power to make the country righteous?
faq.a: The study rules this out at the cross. The church that grabs the sword forgets that its Lord told Peter to put his away. A gospel enforced by the sword is no longer the gospel. That isn't a call to passivity. It means serving the city, paying the tax, honoring the office, and working for justice, while keeping one foot in the kingdom of the crucified King. Caring about the country isn't the error. Believing Christ needs Caesar's sword to finish his work is.

faq.q: Is it wrong to grieve the loss of a Christian culture, the closed stores and the moral consensus?
faq.a: No. The study honors that grief as love looking at a wound. When the culture honored the faith, the unborn, the poor, and marriage had more support, and those were real goods. The harder question is how the church held them, by being the church or by borrowing the state's power. A protection that rests on a majority rather than on changed hearts is always one election from collapse. The deeper work is forming people who would live the mercy when the law no longer requires it.

faq.q: I'm a skeptic. Isn't this just religion arguing about how to grab power?
faq.a: It's a fair suspicion, and the study shares it. Its argument is that the faith of Jesus refuses to advance by seizing the state, that Jesus turned down the kingdoms of the world, and that he took his throne by being executed. If you've seen Christianity used as a tool for power, the study calls that a corruption, whether it shows up as a grab for power or a smug retreat. What it points to instead is the early church, which had no power for three centuries and grew anyway by taking in the people the empire threw away. You don't have to accept the faith to see that this study argues against the very thing you distrust.

faq.q: Does "a kingdom not of this world" mean Jesus didn't care about justice here and now?
faq.a: No. When Jesus told Pilate his kingdom isn't of this world (John 18:36), the proof he gave was that his servants weren't fighting. He wasn't saying his kingdom has nothing to do with this world, only that it doesn't come from here or advance by this world's methods. The same Jesus healed the sick and welcomed the outcast, and the church that followed him nursed the dying and refused to expose its infants. Caring about justice isn't the error. Believing justice only comes when our side seizes the throne is.

faq.q: Does refusing the culture war mean retreating into a Christian bubble?
faq.a: No. The study calls the bubble the mirror image of the culture war, not its cure. The community it points to isn't a bunker but a people so different that the world is drawn to them, who take in the discarded and live differently in public. The early church had no cultural power and was among the most visible communities in the empire. The choice isn't between recapturing the culture and fleeing it. It's being salt, lived in the open.

faq.q: Does this study tell me how to vote?
faq.a: No. A study that gave voting instructions would betray its own argument. Its concern is where your hope rests and whether your faith can still rebuke the side you favor. Two believers who both keep the crucified King above every throne can vote differently in good conscience. The study asks you to honor the office while judging the officeholder, to hold your convictions as a Christian rather than a soldier, and never to put in an election the hope that belongs to Christ.

faq.q: How do I lead this with no seminary training and little time?
faq.a: The way it was built to be led, by a busy volunteer. Every discussion question carries a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer. The teaching, the Scripture notes, and this leader's guide are there so you aren't improvising. The real qualification is willingness to go first, to be truthful about your own heart, and to keep the room safe for people who disagree. Read the leader's guide, settle your own heart, and trust the material.

timeline.event: Jesus is crucified under Pontius Pilate, having told the governor that his kingdom is not of this world.
Fire sweeps Rome and Nero blames the Christians, beginning the first imperial persecution. By tradition, Peter and Paul die in Rome in these years.
Pliny the Younger writes to the emperor Trajan asking how to handle the Christians he has been executing for their refusal to sacrifice.
The martyrs of Lyon are killed, later recorded by Eusebius in his Ecclesiastical History.
The emperor Decius requires citizens to sacrifice to the gods and obtain a certificate proving it.
The Great Persecution under Diocletian begins, with scriptures burned and churches destroyed.
The Edict of Milan, issued by Constantine and Licinius, grants toleration to Christians across the empire.
The Edict of Thessalonica under Theodosius makes Nicene Christianity the official religion of the empire.
Augustine completes The City of God, begun after the sack of Rome in 410, describing two cities formed by two loves.
Luther's treatise on temporal authority sets out his distinction between God's rule through the gospel and through civil government.
The Peace of Westphalia ends Europe's wars of religion, confirming with changes the principle first set at Augsburg in 1555 that a ruler decides his territory's religion.
The Confessing Church issues the Barmen Declaration, drafted largely by Karl Barth, rejecting the idea that any area of life belongs to a lord other than Jesus Christ.
Robert Bellah publishes "Civil Religion in America."
Stanley Hauerwas and William Willimon publish Resident Aliens, reading the end of the Constantinian arrangement as a chance for the church to be faithful again.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thank you for being here. Three things before we start. First, this study asks hard questions of the Christian who wants to seize the culture and the Christian who wants to flee it, and both of those live in most of our hearts, so we're not here to score points. Second, nobody has to perform certainty. You can be unsure out loud, and you can change your mind. Third, I'm in this too. Tonight we're looking at ________. Let me read our passage, and then we'll sit with it for a moment before anyone speaks.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked hard at what the passage and the essay say. Now let's bring it home, off the page and into the week ahead, because none of this matters if it stays an idea.
facilitatorScript.close: We'll stop there, even though it isn't resolved, because some of this shouldn't be wrapped up neatly. Take it with you. Try the practice this week, and spend some time with the reflection questions on your own. Come back ready to be truthful, not finished. Let me pray for us before we go.

bibliography.title: The City of God
bibliography.author: Augustine
bibliography.note: The two cities formed by two loves, mixed together in history, so that no earthly nation is the city of God. Begun after the sack of Rome in 410. Background for sessions 4 and 5.

bibliography.title: The Christians as the Romans Saw Them (1984)
bibliography.author: Robert Louis Wilken
bibliography.note: How educated Romans such as Celsus and Porphyry saw the church as a stubborn, antisocial sect. A fair statement of Rome's case for sessions 1 and 3.

bibliography.title: The Rise of Christianity (1996)
bibliography.author: Rodney Stark
bibliography.note: A sociologist's account of early Christian growth, including the argument that Christians' care for the sick during plagues helped the church grow. Background for session 3; weigh it rather than simply accept it.

bibliography.title: The Ecclesiastical History
bibliography.author: Eusebius
bibliography.note: The early church's own record of the persecutions, including the martyrs of Lyon in 177. Background for session 3.

bibliography.title: The Letters of the Younger Pliny
bibliography.author: Pliny the Younger
bibliography.note: Includes his letter to Trajan around 112 about the Christians in his province. A primary source for session 3.

bibliography.title: The Desire of the Nations: Rediscovering the Roots of Political Theology (1996)
bibliography.author: Oliver O'Donovan
bibliography.note: A serious case that the gospel reshaped political authority in the West. Used to honor the strongest defense of Christendom in sessions 2 and 4.

bibliography.title: Practice in Christianity (1850)
bibliography.author: Søren Kierkegaard
bibliography.note: Kierkegaard on the offense of a crucified Lord and the illusion of a Christendom where everyone is a Christian by default. Background for session 2.

bibliography.title: Resident Aliens: Life in the Christian Colony (1989)
bibliography.author: Stanley Hauerwas and William H. Willimon
bibliography.note: Known for the claim that the church doesn't have a social strategy, the church is a social strategy, and for reading the end of the Constantinian arrangement as an opportunity. One strong voice among several, since this study also supports public engagement.

bibliography.title: Foolishness to the Greeks: The Gospel and Western Culture (1986)
bibliography.author: Lesslie Newbigin
bibliography.note: Written after Newbigin returned to Britain in 1974 and found it a mission field. Asks how the gospel speaks to a culture that thinks it already knows the gospel. Background for session 2.

bibliography.title: The Myth of Religious Violence (2009)
bibliography.author: William T. Cavanaugh
bibliography.note: Argues that the modern story of secular peace served the rise of the state, which cast itself as the referee that ended religious violence. Complicates the two-drawer reading in session 1.

bibliography.title: To Change the World (2010)
bibliography.author: James Davison Hunter
bibliography.note: On how the church lost its place at the cultural center and why its strategies of political conquest served it poorly; proposes faithful presence. Background for session 5.

bibliography.title: Ethics
bibliography.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
bibliography.note: Written during the German church's failure and published after his death, including his criticism of thinking in terms of two separate spheres. Background for session 4.

bibliography.title: The Barmen Theological Declaration (1934)
bibliography.author: Confessing Church, drafted largely by Karl Barth
bibliography.note: The confession that Jesus Christ is the one Word of God we must hear and obey, rejecting the idea that any area of life belongs to other lords. Central to session 4.

furtherReading: Confessions and On Christian Doctrine, Augustine, for the fuller account of rightly ordered love behind the two-kingdoms teaching in session 4.
After Christendom?, Stanley Hauerwas, for readers who want to press session 2's claim that the church doesn't need to run the country.
Defending Constantine, Peter J. Leithart, a serious counter-voice to the simple story that the church was ruined in 312, useful against sessions 2 and 5.
Theopolitical Imagination, William T. Cavanaugh, on the church as its own public rather than a chaplain to the state.
The Rise of Christianity, Rodney Stark, for the social history behind session 3.

glossary.definition: Jesus' answer in Mark 12:17, giving the coin that bears Caesar's image back to Caesar and giving to God what bears God's image, the human person. Often misread as a wall between faith and public life; it's a fence around a coin.

The long arrangement in which Christianity was a civilization's default, built into its laws, calendar, and manners, so that belonging to the culture and to the church felt like the same thing. Distinct from the faith itself, which can outlive it.
The pattern, named for the emperor Constantine, of the church aligning with state power and pursuing its mission through government rather than the way of the cross.

The teaching that God rules the world in two ways, through the church by the word and through the civil order by law and the sword, so the two shouldn't collapse into one. A way of holding a tension, not a wall that silences the church.
The shared beliefs and rituals through which a nation understands itself before God, with its own sacred symbols and holy days. It can humble a nation or flatter it.
The biblical condition of God's people living as a minority under a power not their own, told to seek the city's welfare without mistaking it for home.
Paul's language for the structures, authorities, and spiritual forces that order the world and can become idols when they demand the loyalty owed to God.
Augustine's picture of the earthly city formed by love of self and the city of God formed by love of God, mixed together in this age and told apart by their loves.

glossary.term: Salt that has lost its taste
glossary.definition: Jesus' warning in Matthew 5:13 about salt that can no longer be told apart from what it seasons. A picture of a church so blended into its culture that it can bear witness to nothing beyond it.
Jesus' picture of the kingdom as the smallest of seeds that grows into a tree, promising life from smallness rather than ownership of the field.

The movement in the German Protestant church in the 1930s that resisted the fusion of the gospel with the Nazi state, declaring at Barmen in 1934 that Jesus Christ is the one Word of God to be obeyed.
The witness of Christians who refused the public gesture that would have given the state their final loyalty, and died rather than give Caesar what belonged to Christ.
Treating something other than God as ultimate. The idol is usually a good thing, a country or a culture, asked to be God.
The biblical teaching that every human person bears God's likeness, so that each person belongs to God in a way no coin or empire can claim.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: From a coin held up to trap Jesus to the slow end of the arrangement that made Christianity the West's default religion, the church has always had to learn how to live under power it doesn't hold. This five-session study looks at what we owe Caesar and what we owe God, the three centuries the church grew with no power at all, and what is really ending as the culture stops carrying us. It asks hard questions of both the grab for power and the retreat from public life, and any volunteer can lead it without preparation. Join us as we keep the crucified King above every throne.
promoKit.pulpitAnnouncement: We're starting a five-week study on the church and political power, and before anyone braces for a political fight, hear this: it isn't a campaign for a party, and it isn't a call to abandon public life. It asks hard questions of the Christian who wants to seize the culture and the Christian who wants to flee it, and of all of us. And it asks a simple, hard question: what do we owe Caesar, and what belongs only to God? No homework, and no preparation needed to lead a group. Sign up at the welcome table.
promoKit.inviteCaption: Give the coin back to Caesar. Keep nothing of yourself in his hand. A five-session study on how the church has lived under power from Rome to now, fair to those who want to fight and those who want to flee, and simple enough for anyone to lead. Come as you are.
